chapter_summary:
In SwiftUI, the user interface is a function of your app's state. When the state changes, SwiftUI automatically re-renders the affected parts of your UI. Understanding how to manage this state effectively is fundamental to building dynamic and responsive applications. We begin our journey into advanced data flow with two cornerstone property wrappers: `@State` and `@Binding`.

The `@State` property wrapper is designed for managing simple, local state within a single SwiftUI view. When you declare a property with `@State`, you're telling SwiftUI that this property is a source of truth for the view, and any changes to its value should trigger a re-evaluation of the view's `body` property. This re-evaluation is what causes the UI to update. It's crucial to remember that `@State` is typically used for value types like `Int`, `String`, `Bool`, or `struct`s, and it implies that the view *owns* this piece of data. SwiftUI manages the storage for `@State` properties outside of the view's struct, ensuring that the state persists across view updates and re-creations. For example, if you have a counter that increments when a button is tapped, the `count` variable would be a perfect candidate for `@State`.

Consider a simple counter application. You might declare a state variable like `@State private var tapCount: Int = 0`. The `private` access control is a common best practice for `@State` variables, emphasizing that this state is internal to the view that declares it. While not strictly enforced by the compiler, it reinforces the idea of encapsulation and prevents other parts of your app from directly modifying this view's internal state without going through proper channels. When a button's action closure modifies `tapCount`, SwiftUI detects this change, invalidates the view, and re-renders it, showing the new count. This reactive approach is a core tenet of SwiftUI.

Now, what if you want to pass a piece of state from a parent view down to a child view, and you want the child view to be able to modify that state, with the changes reflecting back in the parent? This is where `@Binding` comes into play. A `@Binding` creates a two-way connection to a source of truth that is *owned by another view*. It doesn't store the data itself; instead, it provides a reference to the data owned by an ancestor view. When the child view modifies the `@Binding` property, it's actually modifying the original `@State` property in the parent view, which then triggers a re-render of both the parent and child views. This is incredibly powerful for creating reusable components.

Imagine a parent view that holds a user's name as `@State`. It then presents a child `EditNameView` that allows the user to type in a new name. Instead of passing the name as a regular `String` (which would be a copy and not allow modification of the parent's state), the parent passes a `Binding<String>` to the child. The child view would declare `@Binding var userName: String`. When the user types into a `TextField` bound to `userName` in the child view, the parent's `@State` variable is updated directly. This establishes a clear and efficient data flow: the parent owns the data, but the child has mutable access to it.

A common mistake beginners make is trying to use `@State` in a child view when they actually need a `@Binding`. If a child view declares `@State var someValue: String` and the parent passes `someParentValue` to it, the child receives a *copy* of `someParentValue`. Any changes the child makes to `someValue` will only affect its local copy, and the parent's `someParentValue` will remain unchanged. To enable the two-way sync, the child must declare `@Binding var someValue: String`, and the parent must pass a binding to its state using the `$` prefix, like `EditNameView(userName: $parentUserName)`. The `$` syntax creates a `Binding` from a `@State` property.

Safety notes: Always consider the ownership of your data. `@State` means the view owns the data. `@Binding` means the view is borrowing access to data owned elsewhere. Misunderstanding this can lead to unexpected UI behavior or data inconsistencies. For complex data types, especially reference types, `@State` might not be the most appropriate choice, which we will explore in subsequent chapters. For simple value types and local state, `@State` is your go-to. For passing mutable access to that state down the hierarchy, `@Binding` is indispensable.

screens.title: State Management with @State and @Binding
screens.subtitle: How SwiftUI treats UI as a function of state and connects parent and child views safely

narration.text: In SwiftUI, the interface you see is always a reflection of underlying state. In this chapter you'll explore two foundational tools: the @State property wrapper, which lets a view own a piece of mutable state, and @Binding, which creates a two-way connection to a source of truth owned elsewhere. You'll learn why @State is stored outside the view struct so values persist across view updates, and how changing a @State value triggers SwiftUI to re-evaluate a view's body and update the UI. We'll also walk through practical examples: a simple counter to show how @State works, refactoring the counter into a child to expose a copy-vs-binding problem, and then fixing that problem with @Binding and the $ prefix. Understanding ownership and the distinction between owning state and borrowing access will help you avoid a common beginner mistake: creating local copies in a child view that do not update the parent. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to choose when a piece of data should be owned by a view, when to pass a binding, and how to structure a simple editable list so changes flow back to the single source of truth.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: @State is for a view to own simple local state; @Binding borrows mutable access to that state from a parent. Changes re-render affected views.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › State Management
State Management with @State and @Binding
Learn ownership, reactivity, and two-way data flow between parent and child views.
In this lesson

You will see how @State declares a view-owned source of truth, why changing it reruns the view body, and how to safely grant mutable access to child views with @Binding.

Why it matters

Correct state ownership prevents stale or out-of-sync UI. Passing bindings keeps a single source of truth while enabling reusable child components.

Explore Key Topics
@State
View-owned value-type state that triggers re-renders when mutated.
@Binding
A two-way reference to a source of truth owned by an ancestor view.
Ownership
Who owns data matters. Choose ownership to avoid copies and mismatches.
Visual Concept

Parent View
Owns @State — single source of truth
Pass a Binding to child using the $ prefix
Quick snapshot
  • Use @State for simple, local value types like Int, String, Bool.
  • Use @Binding when a child needs to read and write state owned by a parent.
  • Changing @State triggers SwiftUI to re-evaluate the view body and update the UI.

screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll practice four concrete skills. First, you will understand how @State lets a view own simple local state and why that ownership is important. That means being able to explain what 'source of truth' means and why a view owning a value prevents accidental copies. Second, you'll see how changes to @State trigger view re-evaluation and UI updates; you'll recognize when a mutated value causes SwiftUI to refresh part or all of a view hierarchy. Third, you'll learn how @Binding creates a two-way connection to an externally owned value and how the $ prefix turns a state into a binding that can be passed to children. Finally, you will be able to differentiate use cases: when to keep state locally with @State and when to expose it to children with @Binding. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check your understanding against an explicit outcome.

You will implement a simple task list where the parent holds an array of task strings as @State, and children display and edit each task with a binding. screens.title: @State — What it is and who owns the data
screens.subtitle: The view as the owner of local, value-type state

narration.text: Start by defining @State precisely. @State is a property wrapper used to declare a local, mutable piece of data that a SwiftUI view owns. When a view marks a property with @State, SwiftUI stores that value outside the view struct so the value persists across view re-creation. The view is the source of truth for that state. Practically this means you should pick @State for simple value types such as Int, String, Bool, or small structs that are edited within a single view. A concrete example is a counter: the view owns an integer tapCount as @State. When a user taps a button and the action increments tapCount, SwiftUI detects the change and re-evaluates the view body, updating the displayed count. A common misconception is thinking @State is a global or shared store; it is not. It is explicitly local to the declaring view, and other views that need to read or write that value should receive a binding, not a copy. Finally, a practical guideline: mark @State properties private whenever possible to communicate ownership and to prevent other code from mutating the view’s internal state directly.

keyIdea.title: @State ownership
keyIdea.text: @State declares a view-owned source of truth for simple, local value-type data. Mark it private to show ownership.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › @State — What it is
Definition

@State declares a simple, local piece of mutable state that the view owns. SwiftUI stores it outside the view struct so it persists across updates.

Why ownership matters
  • Owning state prevents accidental overwrites from other views.
  • It clarifies who is allowed to mutate a value and where re-renders originate.
  • Value-type storage fits common UI state: toggles, counters, text fields.
Key Takeaway

@State should own simple, local data. Use private to show intent and avoid external mutation.

Concrete example
@State private var tapCount: Int = 0

// When a button increments tapCount, SwiftUI re-evaluates body and updates the UI.
Misconception
@State is not a shared or global store. It is local to the declaring view. To share or allow mutability from a child, pass a binding instead.

screens.title: How @State changes trigger view re-renders
screens.subtitle: From mutation to UI update: the reactivity loop

narration.text: Understand the reactive loop: when a @State variable changes, SwiftUI marks the view as needing an update and re-evaluates the view's body. This is not manual DOM-style mutation; it is declarative: you change values, and SwiftUI recomputes what the UI should look like. The practical sequence is three steps: (1) mutate the @State wrapped value, usually inside an action closure, (2) SwiftUI detects the write and invalidates the view’s current body, and (3) the framework re-evaluates the body and updates the rendered UI to match the new state. A concrete example is a counter: pressing an increment action writes to tapCount; SwiftUI re-runs the view’s body and the Text showing the count updates. A common source of confusion is thinking every property mutation causes a full app refresh. In reality, SwiftUI attempts to minimize updates and only re-evaluates affected views. Another nuance is that @State storage lives outside the struct, so the view object can be recreated frequently without losing the state value. This storage model explains why @State works reliably even as SwiftUI rebuilds view values during layout and transitions.

keyIdea.title: Reactive loop
keyIdea.text: Mutate @State → SwiftUI invalidates view body → Framework re-evaluates and updates the UI to reflect the new state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Reactivity Loop
The three-step process
1. Mutate @State
An action writes a new value to the wrapped property.
2. Invalidate view body
SwiftUI detects the write and marks the view as needing a refresh.
3. Re-evaluate and update UI
The framework recomputes the view body and updates the visible UI.
Practical note
SwiftUI optimizes updates; it doesn't necessarily redraw the entire screen. The system aims to refresh only affected parts of the view hierarchy.
Concrete example
@State private var tapCount: Int = 0

Button("Tap") {
  tapCount += 1
}
Text("Taps: \(tapCount)")
Misconception check
Do not assume writing to any variable will trigger a SwiftUI update. Only properties wrapped with state-related wrappers such as @State or bindings produce this reactive behavior.

screens.title: Counter example using @State
screens.subtitle: See a simple counter implemented with a view-owned state

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal counter app that demonstrates @State in action. The parent view declares @State private var count: Int = 0 and renders a text label showing the count and a control to increment it. When the user triggers the increment, the action directly mutates count. Because count is wrapped with @State, SwiftUI stores the value outside the view struct and then re-evaluates the body so the displayed value updates. This pattern shows the essential pieces: ownership, mutation, and re-render. A concrete code example helps make this explicit and portable. Notice the private access control on the state variable; it's a best practice to signal the data is internal to the view. A common beginner error is to try to put @State on complex reference types or to expect @State to synchronize automatically between sibling views; @State is intended for local, simple value-type state. After seeing this code, you'll be ready to refactor the increment control into a child view and observe what happens when you pass a plain Int instead of a binding. Counter example using @State means a view-owned integer wrapped by @state persists and triggers ui updates when mutated by user actions.. In practical terms, see a simple counter implemented with a view-owned state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Counter pattern
keyIdea.text: A view-owned integer wrapped by @State persists and triggers UI updates when mutated by user actions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Counter Example
Minimal Counter
struct CounterView: View {
  @State private var count: Int = 0

  var body: some View {
    VStack {
      Text("Count: \(count)")
      Button("Increment") {
        count += 1
      }
    }
  }
}
Why it works

count is owned by the view. Mutating it triggers SwiftUI to recalculate the view body and update the displayed count.

Refactor plan
If you extract the Increment button into a child and pass count as a plain Int, the child will receive a copy. Its taps will change the copy only and the parent will not reflect the updates. The fix is to pass a binding instead so the child can write back to the parent's state.
Pro tip

Use private on @State to clearly communicate ownership and prevent accidental external writes.

screens.title: Passing a plain value vs a Binding
screens.subtitle: Why a child that receives a copy cannot update the parent's state

narration.text: This screen contrasts two approaches to passing data to a child view. First, passing a plain value: when the parent passes a value type like Int or String to a child as a regular parameter, the child receives a copy. If the child mutates that value or provides a TextField bound to a local variable, those changes affect only the child's local copy and do not alter the parent's source of truth. This breaks the expectation of synchronized state. Second, passing a binding: the parent uses the $ prefix to provide a Binding to its @State property. The child declares @Binding for that parameter and writes through the binding; when it does, the parent's @State value is updated and SwiftUI re-renders both views as needed. A concrete mistake beginners make is declaring @State in the child to hold a copy of a parent value. This creates two independent owners and leads to confusing UI. The correct pattern for shared mutable access is a single owner and borrowed bindings for children. Passing a plain value vs a Binding means passing a plain value creates a copy; passing a binding borrows mutable access to the parent's source of truth.. In practical terms, why a child that receives a copy cannot update the parent's state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Copy vs Borrow
keyIdea.text: Passing a plain value creates a copy; passing a binding borrows mutable access to the parent's source of truth.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Copy vs Binding
Passing a plain value
// Parent
let value = 5
ChildView(number: value)

// Child
struct ChildView: View {
  var number: Int // copy
}
Result: child has a copy. Mutations in the child do not affect the parent’s state. This leads to stale or desynchronized UI if you expected two-way updates.
Passing a binding
// Parent
@State private var count = 0
ChildView(count: $count)

// Child
struct ChildView: View {
  @Binding var count: Int
}
Result: child writes through the binding and updates the parent's @State. The UI reflects changes in both views consistently.
Common mistake

Declaring @State in a child to try to mutate a parent value creates separate owners and breaks synchronization. Use @Binding instead.

screens.title: @Binding — Two-way connection to a source of truth
screens.subtitle: Borrow mutable access to state owned by an ancestor view

narration.text: A @Binding creates a two-way connection to a value owned by another view. Unlike @State, a binding does not store data. Instead, it provides read and write access to a source of truth elsewhere in the view hierarchy. To create a binding, the parent supplies the $ prefix in front of its @State variable, for example $userName, and the child declares @Binding var userName: String. When the child modifies that binding, the parent's @State value changes and SwiftUI triggers re-evaluation of affected views. A concrete use case is a child view with a TextField that edits a parent's string. The binding pattern makes small, reusable components possible because the component does not own the data it edits. Keep in mind that bindings should be used when you want the child to mutate the parent's state; if the child only needs to display data and not modify it, prefer passing an immutable value. Also remember ownership: the parent remains the single source of truth even while the child borrows mutable access. @Binding — Two-way connection to a source of truth means bindings give children direct read/write access to another view's state while leaving ownership with the parent.. In practical terms, borrow mutable access to state owned by an ancestor view. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: @Binding summary
keyIdea.text: Bindings give children direct read/write access to another view's state while leaving ownership with the parent.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › @Binding — Two-way
Definition & Use

@Binding declares a borrowed, mutable reference to a value owned elsewhere. The parent passes a binding with the $ prefix.

Example pattern
// Parent
@State private var name = ""
ChildEditView(name: $name)

// Child
struct ChildEditView: View {
  @Binding var name: String
  var body: some View { TextField("Name", text: $name) }
}
Why this is powerful
  • It keeps a single source of truth in the parent while letting children mutate it safely.
  • It enables small, reusable controls that operate on externally provided state.
  • Bindings avoid copies and ensure updates propagate back to the owner immediately.
Key Takeaway

Use @Binding when a child must read and write a parent's state. Parent retains ownership; child borrows access.

screens.title: EditNameView example using @Binding
screens.subtitle: How a child TextField updates a parent's @State string

narration.text: Let's examine a concrete child view that edits a parent's string through a binding. The parent holds @State private var userName: String and passes a binding to the child by calling EditNameView(userName: $userName). The child declares @Binding var userName: String and binds a TextField to $userName. When the user types, the TextField writes through the binding back to the parent's @State, and the parent's UI updates instantly. This demonstrates three important points: the child does not own the data, changes in the child are reflected in the parent, and the $ prefix in the parent creates the binding that the child expects. A typical beginner fix is to replace a copy-in-child approach with this pattern. When you read code like this, mentally identify the source of truth — the parent’s @State property — and treat the child as a controlled component that borrows access to it. That mental model makes it easier to reason about the flow of updates in your app. EditNameView example using @Binding means parent owns the string as @state; child consumes it as @binding and updates the parent through the binding.. In practical terms, how a child textfield updates a parent's @state string. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: EditName pattern
keyIdea.text: Parent owns the string as @State; child consumes it as @Binding and updates the parent through the binding.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › EditNameView
Parent & Child
// Parent
@State private var name: String = "Alice"
EditNameView(userName: $name)

// Child
struct EditNameView: View {
  @Binding var userName: String
  var body: some View {
    TextField("Edit name", text: $userName)
  }
}
This pattern keeps one authoritative source of truth while allowing child controls to mutate it directly.
Concrete behavior
  • Typing in the TextField immediately updates the parent's name value.
  • SwiftUI re-evaluates both parent and child bodies as needed so the UI stays consistent.
  • This enables small reusable editor components that operate on externally provided state.
Pro tip

When a child only reads data, pass an immutable value. Use bindings only when the child will write.

screens.title: Parent-controlled lists and ForEach with bindings
screens.subtitle: Using $items to pass bindings into repeated child views

narration.text: When your parent owns a collection of items in @State, and you want each child to edit its corresponding element, SwiftUI provides a concise pattern: use ForEach over a binding collection. By writing ForEach($items, id: \. self) { $item in... } you obtain a binding to each element inside the loop. The child view can then accept @Binding var taskDescription: String and edit the string directly. This avoids copying the array element into the child and preserves a single source of truth in the parent. A concrete hands-on example is the TaskListView from the chapter: the parent keeps @State private var tasks: [String] and passes each binding to TaskEditView. Editing a task in the child updates the parent's array immediately, and deleting or adding tasks updates the list consistently. One important note: use stable identifiers in ForEach when working with custom types to avoid identity surprises. For simple strings, using the element itself as id can be acceptable for demonstration, but in real apps a unique id per item is safer. Parent-controlled lists and ForEach with bindings means use foreach($items, id:\.self) or bind to elements by id to give children direct access to individual elements of a parent-owned collection.. In practical terms, using $items to pass bindings into repeated child views. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bindings in collections
keyIdea.text: Use ForEach($items, id:\.self) or bind to elements by id to give children direct access to individual elements of a parent-owned collection.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Bindings in lists
Task list pattern

Parent owns tasks as an array of strings. Use ForEach over $tasks to get bindings into each element so children edit the source directly.

// Parent
@State private var tasks: [String] = ["Buy groceries", "Walk the dog"]

List {
  ForEach($tasks, id: \.self) { $task in
    TaskEditView(taskDescription: $task)
  }
}

// Child
struct TaskEditView: View {
  @Binding var taskDescription: String
  var body: some View { TextField("Edit task", text: $taskDescription) }
}
Why use bindings here?
  • Children edit the exact element inside the parent's collection.
  • The parent remains the single source of truth for the list content.
  • Adding or deleting items in the parent updates the list correctly for all children.
Key Takeaway

ForEach over $collection gives each iteration a binding to the element, enabling direct edits that update the source array.

screens.title: Ownership rules and best practices
screens.subtitle: When to use @State, when to use @Binding, and access control

narration.text: This lesson consolidates ownership rules and practical guidelines. Rule one: the owner of a piece of mutable state should be the single source of truth. Use @State when a view is the natural owner of simple, local state. Rule two: when a child must modify that state, pass a binding so the child borrows access without taking ownership. Rule three: mark @State properties private when possible to make the ownership explicit and prevent accidental external mutation. Rule four: avoid declaring @State for complex shared data models; for those cases consider observable objects and other patterns discussed in later chapters. A useful heuristic is to ask: will only this view ever mutate this data? If yes, use @State. If other views need to mutate it, keep the owner at the highest logical point in the hierarchy and pass bindings or use shared observable models as appropriate. These ownership decisions make your UI predictable and prevent bugs caused by multiple independent copies of the same data. Ownership rules and best practices means single source of truth: owner should hold @state; children borrow with @binding. mark state private to communicate ownership.. In practical terms, when to use @state, when to use @binding, and access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rules
keyIdea.text: Single source of truth: owner should hold @State; children borrow with @Binding. Mark state private to communicate ownership.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Ownership rules
Best practices
  • Prefer @State for simple, local, value-type state owned by one view.
  • Use @Binding for child views that need to mutate an ancestor's state.
  • Mark @State private to show the view owns the data and restrict external writes.
  • For complex shared data or reference types, consider observable objects instead of @State.
Decision checklist
• Does only this view need to mutate the value? Use @State.
• Do children need writable access? Keep the owner in the parent and pass @Binding.
• Is the data complex and shared widely? Consider other state management tools in later chapters.
Caveat

Using @State for large reference types can be inefficient or misleading; prefer patterns designed for shared models.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build a Task List with editable items
screens.subtitle: Parent owns the list; children edit tasks via bindings

narration.text: Now put the ideas together with a hands-on example you can run in Xcode. The parent view holds @State private var tasks: [String] and renders a List containing ForEach($tasks, id: \. self) { $task in TaskEditView(taskDescription: $task) }. The child TaskEditView declares @Binding var taskDescription: String and uses a TextField bound to $taskDescription. When you edit the field, the parent's tasks array updates instantly. The parent can also add and delete tasks by modifying the @State array; those changes are reflected in the list and in each child. This pattern demonstrates clean ownership: the parent is the single source of truth and children are controlled components that borrow access. While implementing, test the behavior: edit a task and verify the parent’s array changes, add a task and confirm a new child appears, and delete an item to see the list update. This activity reinforces the ownership, binding, and re-render concepts in a practical, repeatable way. Hands-on: Build a Task List with editable items means parent owns tasks as @state; children edit each element through bindings provided by foreach over $tasks.. In practical terms, parent owns the list; children edit tasks via bindings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on pattern
keyIdea.text: Parent owns tasks as @State; children edit each element through bindings provided by ForEach over $tasks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Task List Lab
Starter code
// Parent
@State private var tasks: [String] = ["Buy groceries", "Walk the dog"]

List {
  ForEach($tasks, id: \.self) { $task in
    TaskEditView(taskDescription: $task)
  }
}

// Child
struct TaskEditView: View {
  @Binding var taskDescription: String
  var body: some View {
    HStack {
      TextField("Edit task", text: $taskDescription)
      Text("Current: \(taskDescription)")
    }
  }
}
Try this
  1. Edit a task in the child and observe the parent’s array update in the debugger or a printed log.
  2. Add a new task from the parent and confirm a new child appears for editing.
  3. Delete a task and verify indices and bindings remain consistent.
Key Takeaway

Use ForEach over $collection to hand children bindings to their element so edits update the parent source of truth.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.subtitle: Avoid copies, be mindful of ownership, and choose the right wrapper

narration.text: This final lesson highlights common pitfalls and safety considerations. First, avoid declaring @State in a child when you intended to let the parent remain the owner. Doing so creates a separate local state and leads to desynchronized UI. Second, be careful when using value identity as the ForEach id — for complex or mutable items prefer stable unique identifiers to prevent visual glitches when items reorder. Third, remember that @State is ideal for simple value types; for large reference models or widely shared data, other tools such as observable objects are more appropriate and will be covered later. Fourth, the $ prefix is how you create a Binding from a @State property; forgetting the $ leads to compile errors or copying. Finally, always reason about who owns the data and put the owner as high as necessary in the hierarchy so that all interested children can receive bindings or read-only values. These practices will keep your UI predictable and aligned with SwiftUI's declarative model. Mistake: Child @State
Declaring @State in the child to try to update the parent creates two ownerships and breaks synchronization. Use @Binding instead.
Mistake: Unstable ForEach ids
Using mutable values as ids can confuse SwiftUI when items reorder. Prefer stable unique ids for custom types.
Safety note
For complex or widely shared data, a single @State per view may not be appropriate. Learn ObservableObject and environment patterns in later chapters.
